newsitem.title: USA: "Euro-phoria" tempered by words of caution at IMF.
newsitem.headline: "Euro-phoria" tempered by words of caution at IMF.

text.p: Unfettered "euro-optimism" at the spring meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank was tempered on Tuesday by words of caution from several private bankers, who warned that many obstacles to the single currency's launch remain.

The European Union's commissioner of monetary affairs, Yves-Thibault de Silguy, said he expected the planned euro currency to be as stable as the German mark is now, and repeated his belief that European monetary union was irreversible.

"The euro will be a sound and therefore an attractive currency," he said, predicting that it would account for a greater share of central bank reserves than the portion currently taken up by European currencies.
De Silguy was speaking at an Institute of International Finance conference on the last day of the IMF spring meetings.

On Monday, de Silguy dismissed concerns that France or Germany would fail to meet the Maastricht criteria for monetary union and also ruled out the possibility of a weakening of the guidelines -- something French Socialists have suggested they will push for if they win upcoming parliamentary elections.
But a series of top international private bankers, also speaking at the conference, expressed greater scepticism about the euro's prospects.
"I am afraid the markets have been carried away with euro-phoria," said Ulrich Cartellieri, a member of Deutsche Bank's management board.
He predicted Germany would meet the EMU criteria, provided certain critical conditions were met, but cautioned that it would be "a walk on a razored edge."
Cartellieri questioned whether markets were experiencing a "calm before the storm," and said a number of problems were lurking.

He said a reopening of the debate on whether Italy will be allowed to enter in the first wave of EMU, and the prospect of renewed political debate on EMU following French elections in May and early June would affect financial markets.
"Even assuming EMU starts on time, I still think things are going to be bumpy," Cartellieri said.
John Lipsky, chief economist and director of research at Chase Manhattan Bank, voiced confidence on the euro's implications for heightened competitiveness within Europe.
But he also said that there remained key questions about the stability pact, public acceptance of the euro and the method for fixing exchange rates.

"Significant issues remain uncertain that have important implications for the euro and its impact on markets," said Lipsky. "The euro's full potential will not be achieved overnight." REUTER 292254 GMT apr 97
